_notes: Per explicit instruction: advanced rules are always incorporated, not a togglable option. This file exists to make which specific rules that means auditable, not to make it optional at runtime.

official.description: Core rules as printed in the base GF9 rulebook. Always active regardless of advanced/standard.

advanced.description: Rules the base rulebook itself labels Advanced Game. Always active per project instruction, this is not a runtime toggle.

doubleSpiceBlow.notes: Two Spice Cards revealed per Spice Blow phase instead of one, with two separate discard piles (A and B). Each resolves independently, including its own possible Nexus.

strongholdSpiceCollection.notes: Passive income just for occupying at the time of collection, stacks if a faction occupies more than one qualifying stronghold. Independent of the normal 2/3-spice-per-force collection rate for territories with an active spice blow.

combatSpiceSupport.notes: Each force in a battle counts at full strength only if 1 spice is committed to it; uncommitted forces count at half strength. Battle Plan must declare total spice expended alongside the dialed number. Spice goes to the Spice Bank regardless of win/loss, except when a Traitor is revealed (winner owes nothing).

karamaCards.notes: In addition to the base-game effect (cancel one opponent faction advantage for the phase), advanced Karama grants each faction a unique one-time power on play. Bene Gesserit has no advanced Karama power in the base game. Full per-faction power table needs transcribing into rulesConfig or a dedicated karamaPowers.json before the bidding/battle engine can implement it, not yet done here.

expansionAdvanced.description: Advanced-game additions from the two expansions, same always-on treatment once an expansion faction is in play.

leaderSkillCards.notes: CHOAM & Richese variant, opt-in per rulebook rather than always-on, not a base advanced rule. Leaving disabled by default, revisit if wanted.

advancedStrongholdCards.notes: Same as Leader Skill Cards, an opt-in variant rather than a base advanced rule.

optional.description: True optional/variant rules (not the base game's own Advanced Game section). Off by default, distinct from the always-on advanced rules above.
optional.notes: The rulebook's Optional Rules for Alliances table (page 24) offers five named presets. Default is the original unrestricted alliance game. Worth a decision later, not urgent for Phase 1.

implementationDecisions.description: Rules that exist only because a physical-table interaction needs a digital equivalent. Every entry here must have a one-line justification so it's auditable later.

entries.justification: Atreides Prescience at the table: Atreides asks one question and the opponent must then play what they revealed. Digitally the opponent locks their whole plan first and Atreides is shown the named element before locking. Equivalent outcome, and it removes any chance of the revealed answer being changed afterwards.

Physical bidding relies on players holding cards face down; digital equivalent is a sequential reveal-and-decide UI rather than simultaneous entry, to preserve bidding psychology per section 16 of the brief.
The original Avalon Hill rules say the Voice cannot name a Cheap Hero; the GF9 2019 rules list Cheap Heroes among valid Voice commands. GF9 is this project's authority, so Cheap Heroes can be voiced.

A submitted battle plan that breaks a rule (a card not in hand, a leader already used in another territory) is replaced by a minimal legal plan rather than halting the game. The human panel prevents this for players; it guards against AI bugs.
After a Harkonnen win, the winner's keep/discard choice is resolved before the capture. The two are independent in the rules; a fixed order keeps the digital flow simple.

At the table, Nexus negotiation is free conversation. Digitally it runs in turn order: each allied faction may break away, then each unallied faction may propose to one other unallied faction, who accepts or rejects. Every faction gets a say, and no alliance forms without both sides agreeing.
Revealing a traitor is optional in the rules. The holder (or, for a Harkonnen traitor used for an ally, Harkonnen) is asked once plans are revealed; the AI always reveals.

Advanced rules: after the first storm, the Fremen reveal the Storm card they previewed last turn, then shuffle all six back and preview the next. The six cards are modelled as values 1 to 6, one each (js/stormEngine.js STORM_DECK), pending confirmation against the physical deck. Without the Fremen in play, the last two battlers dial 1-3 each as in the basic rules.

House rule at the project owner's request. Officially Atreides look at the top Spice card during Shipment and Movement; here they see it from the end of the Spice Blow. The card cannot change in between (nothing is drawn until the next Spice Blow), so Atreides simply know it earlier, during Bidding and Revival.

The official rules allow no voluntary discards. Weather Control and Family Atomics need the storm's sector data and have no use yet, so their holders may discard them (the human from the Hand sheet, the AI at the start of Bidding). Remove once the storm is built.

Truthtrance allows any yes/no question answered truthfully. Digitally, questions are limited to facts the game can answer from its own state (do you hold a kind of card, is this leader your traitor, do you have at least N spice), in line with tournament guidance to avoid speculative questions. The game answers, so answers are always truthful.

Karama's core use is built: cancelling the Voice, Atreides Prescience or a Harkonnen capture as it is used against you. Other Karama cancels and each faction's once-per-game advanced Karama power are not yet built.

Allies may pay for each other's treachery cards and shipments. Digitally, at the start of Bidding each allied faction may pledge an amount for that turn; the ally spends its own spice first, then the pledge.

House rule at the project owner's request: the five worthless cards (Baliset, Jubba Cloak, Kulon, La La La, Trip to Gamont) are left out of the Treachery Deck, making 28 cards instead of 33. Their rules remain in the code (bluffing in battle, Bene Gesserit using them as Karama); set houseRules.removeWorthlessCards to false to restore them. Games already in progress keep their deck.

Standing in for the board's printed sectors (project owner's rule): each territory lies mostly in one storm sector, computed from this game's own map with the storm wedge's angles (tools/computeSectors.py, stormSector in data/territories.json). The storm destroys all forces and spice in every SAND territory whose sector it passes over or stops in. Stone territories and strongholds are immune; Imperial Basin is sheltered by the Shield Wall (rulebook); the Polar Sink is never in the storm; the Fremen lose half their forces, rounded up (advanced).

What you see is what you can move across. Borders (adjacentDraft in data/territories.json, used for all movement, Fremen free shipping, worm rides and the AI) are computed from this game's own map outlines by tools/computeBorders.py: two territories border when they share at least 66px of edge. Every corner contact measured 60px or less and every real edge 72px or more, so the cut-off separates them cleanly. The original rulebook list is kept as adjacentBoard for reference.

House rules at the project owner's request, to see how games play when they can drag on: no 10-turn limit (play continues until a stronghold victory), no Spacing Guild special victory, the Fremen special victory kept as a one-time check at the end of turn 10 (it is defined at the last turn), and a draw if nobody has won by the end of turn 30 (houseRules.stalemateTurnCap) so a true stalemate cannot run forever. Set houseRules.noTurnLimit and noGuildSpecialVictory to false to restore the official game.

Expansion plan decision D1 (project owner): the worthless cards return to the deck only when something in the game needs them (CHOAM seated, Leader Skills or Stronghold Cards on); otherwise the house rule removing them stands.
Expansion plan decision D5 (project owner): CHOAM collects spice for every player in the game during Charity, so it can always pay other factions' charity; no shortfall rule is needed.
Expansion plan decision D7 (project owner): Ixian Cyborgs have no separate revival cap; they count toward the normal limit of 3 forces a turn.

Any 2 to 6 factions may play (GF9 supports 2 to 6 players). Seating follows the board order; the traitor deck only contains leaders of factions in play. Verified by 60 simulated games across every line-up size with no crashes or invariant breaks.

Ixians & Tleilaxu battle cards (expansion plan M1): each card's effect comes from what it counts as in its slot (battleEngine.slotKinds). Poison Blade is projectile and poison (only a Shield Snooper stops it); Weirding Way in the defence slot beside a weapon is a projectile defence; Chemistry in the weapon slot beside a defence is a poison weapon; Shield Snooper is both defences and counts as a Shield for Lasgun explosions and Artillery; Poison Tooth kills both leaders (not stopped by a Snooper) unless its owner withholds it after the reveal, and is discarded if used; Artillery Strike kills both leaders unless shielded, surviving leaders do not count, no spice is paid for the kills, and it is always discarded. The Voice names card types, and a card counts as every type it is. Controlled by expansions.ixTlCards.

Ixians & Tleilaxu special cards (M1 part 2). Sandtrout (spice deck): cancels all alliances; the next Shai-Hulud still devours but brings no Nexus; the card after it doubles its spice, or if another worm brings the Nexus. Thumper: at the start of the Spice Blow (not turn 1), pile A resolves as though Shai-Hulud had appeared, then draws on. Harvester: doubles a blow placed this phase, if still on the board (offered just after the reveals). Amal: every faction discards half its spice rounded up; the AI is offered it at the start of Bidding, the human plays it from the Hand between phases. Kull Wahad is worthless and enters only with worthless cards (D1). The Cheap Hero traitor matches any Cheap Hero an opponent plays and stays in its holder's hand.

Tleilaxu (expansion M2, core). Start: 20 forces in reserve, 5 spice, 2 free revivals, nothing on Arrakis. No traitors: after the others choose, the Tleilaxu draw 3 Face Dancers from the traitor deck. When ANOTHER faction wins a battle with a Face Dancer leader, the Tleilaxu may reveal it: the win stands, the leader goes to the tanks (no spice for it), the winner's remaining forces there return to reserves and are replaced by Tleilaxu forces from reserve (up to the same number; taking forces from elsewhere on the planet is not yet offered). All three revealed: recycle and draw three new. Mentat Pause: may swap one unrevealed Face Dancer. Revival (advanced): other factions pay the Tleilaxu; the Tleilaxu revive with no limit at half price (rounded up) to the Bank and take 1 spice for each faction using free revival or a Ghola card; they may raise a faction's limit to 5 for the turn; their ally revives at half price. Zoal takes the value of the opposing leader disc (0 against a Cheap Hero). Not yet: Gholas, leader-price negotiation, Karama powers.

Ixians (expansion M3, core). Start: 10 spice; 3 Cyborgs + 3 Suboids in the Hidden Mobile Stronghold, 4 Cyborgs + 10 Suboids in reserve (Cyborgs are the starred forces); 1 free revival. Cyborgs: worth 2 in battle, cost 3 to revive, no separate revival cap (D7). Suboids: worth half and never boosted with spice. Groups with a Cyborg move 2, Suboids alone 1 (ornithopters still give 3). HMS: a stronghold territory ('hms') linked only to the territory it points at; placed after the first storm on any non-stronghold territory not in storm; counts for victory; immune to storm and worms; before each storm (turn 2+), while Ixians occupy it, it may move up to 3 territories between non-stronghold territories, never into, out of or through storm, collecting up to 2 spice per Ixian force inside from each spice territory entered; only the Ixians ship straight in, others enter from its host. Starting draft: Ixians choose from one card per faction. Bidding: the Ixians see the auction cards plus one, and put one back on the top or bottom of the deck. Alliance: the ally may swap a card just bought for the top card. Not yet: Technology, Suboids replacing lost Cyborgs, Ixian Karama powers.

victoryVariants.notes: Confirmed directly from the base rulebook text. Solo win is 3 strongholds (or all 3 Tech Tokens if Ixian/Tleilaxu expansion is active, per that expansion's rulebook), alliance win is 4 (first player) held jointly. Two-player games use 4 regardless of alliance status.
